title: Problem Overview: Polynomial Interpolation Bound
content: Erdős Problem #1133 (OPEN, 1967) asks: given any sample points in [-1,1], can we always choose target values y_i in [-1,1] such that ANY polynomial of degree < (1+ε)n passing through ≥ (1-ε)n of the points (x_i, y_i) must satisfy max|P(x)| > C on [-1,1]? The quantifier order is adversarial: we choose y_i after seeing x_i but before seeing P.
mathContext: The conjecture has five nested quantifiers: $\forall C > 0,\; \exists \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N,\; \forall n \geq N,\; \forall x_1,\ldots,x_n \in [-1,1],\; \exists y_1,\ldots,y_n \in [-1,1]$ such that $\forall P$ with $\deg P < (1+\varepsilon)n$ matching $\geq (1-\varepsilon)n$ points: $\|P\|_{\infty, [-1,1]} > C$. The difficulty lies in the $\exists y \forall P$ ordering — choosing $y$ before seeing $P$ requires a strategy that defeats ALL polynomials simultaneously.

title: Imports and Setup
content: Imports Polynomial.Basic and Polynomial.Eval for polynomial arithmetic and evaluation, Real.cos for Chebyshev nodes, and Finset.Basic for counting interpolation matches. Opens the Polynomial namespace for cleaner syntax.
mathContext: Mathlib's $\texttt{Polynomial ℝ}$ represents polynomials as $\texttt{Finsupp ℕ ℝ}$ (finite support functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$). The $\texttt{eval}$ function evaluates $P(x) = \sum_{i} a_i x^i$. The $\texttt{natDegree}$ field gives the largest index with nonzero coefficient.

title: polyEval — Polynomial Evaluation
content: Wrapper around P.eval x for polynomial evaluation at a real point. Syntactic convenience for the formalization.
mathContext: For $P = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i X^i \in \mathbb{R}[X]$, $\texttt{polyEval}(P, x) = P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i x^i$. This is a ring homomorphism: $\texttt{eval}(P \cdot Q, x) = \texttt{eval}(P, x) \cdot \texttt{eval}(Q, x)$.

title: maxNormOnInterval — Chebyshev (L∞) Norm
content: The maximum of |P(x)| over x in [-1,1], defined via sSup. This is the Chebyshev norm ‖P‖_{∞,[-1,1]}, the natural measure of polynomial size on an interval. Well-defined since continuous functions on compact sets attain their maximum.
mathContext: The Chebyshev norm $\|P\|_{\infty} = \sup_{x \in [-1,1]} |P(x)|$ is achieved at some $x^* \in [-1,1]$ by the extreme value theorem (continuous $P$ on compact $[-1,1]$). For the Chebyshev polynomial $T_n$, $\|T_n\|_{\infty} = 1$ and $T_n$ attains $\pm 1$ at $n+1$ points — this equioscillation characterizes best approximation.

title: SamplePoints and TargetValues
content: SamplePoints n and TargetValues n are subtypes of Fin n → ℝ restricted to [-1,1]. They represent the sample locations x_i and chosen target values y_i for the interpolation game.
mathContext: Defined as $\{f : \texttt{Fin } n \to \mathbb{R} \mid \forall i,\; -1 \leq f(i) \leq 1\}$. The adversary (nature) chooses $x_i \in [-1,1]$ first; the player then chooses $y_i \in [-1,1]$ to maximize the minimum polynomial norm. This is a minimax problem: $\sup_y \inf_P \|P\|_{\infty}$ subject to the interpolation and degree constraints.

title: ApproximatelyInterpolates
content: P approximately interpolates (x, y) with tolerance ε if P passes through at least (1-ε)n of the points exactly. The subset S of matched indices has |S| ≥ n - ⌊εn⌋. This allows the polynomial to 'miss' up to εn points.
mathContext: Formally: $\exists S \subseteq \texttt{Fin } n,\; |S| \geq n - \lfloor \varepsilon n \rfloor \wedge \forall i \in S,\; P(x_i) = y_i$. For $\varepsilon = 0$: exact interpolation through all $n$ points. The slack $\varepsilon n$ missed points is crucial — it prevents the adversary from simply choosing $y_i$ that make exact interpolation impossible, and gives the polynomial extra freedom.

title: HasBoundedDegree
content: P has bounded degree if natDegree(P) < ⌊(1+ε)n⌋. The polynomial has slightly more than n degrees of freedom (coefficients), giving it flexibility beyond exact interpolation.
mathContext: A polynomial of degree $d$ has $d+1$ free coefficients. With $d < (1+\varepsilon)n$, the polynomial has $\sim (1+\varepsilon)n$ degrees of freedom but only needs to match $\sim (1-\varepsilon)n$ points — leaving $\sim 2\varepsilon n$ excess degrees of freedom. The conjecture claims this excess is NOT enough to keep $\|P\|_{\infty}$ bounded.

title: ErdosConjecture1133 — The Formal Statement
content: The conjecture as a Lean Prop with five nested quantifiers. For any target norm C > 0, there exists tolerance ε > 0 and threshold N such that for n ≥ N, for ANY sample points, there EXIST target values forcing ALL bounded-degree approximately-interpolating polynomials to exceed C on [-1,1].
mathContext:
The game-theoretic structure: $\forall C > 0,\; \exists \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N,\; \forall n \geq N:$ $$\forall \mathbf{x} \in [-1,1]^n,\; \exists \mathbf{y} \in [-1,1]^n,\; \forall P \in \mathbb{R}[X]:\; [\deg P < (1+\varepsilon)n \wedge P \text{ matches } \geq (1-\varepsilon)n \text{ pts}] \implies \|P\|_{\infty} > C.$$
Erdős noted he could not prove this even for $\varepsilon = 0$ (exact interpolation). The conjecture is equivalent to asking: does the min-max interpolation game always favor the 'target chooser'?

title: Erdős's Weaker Result (Known)
content: Erdős proved: for any C > 0, there exists ε > 0 such that for large n and m = ⌊(1+ε)n⌋ sample points, there EXISTS a degree-n polynomial P with |P(x_i)| ≤ 1 at all m points yet ‖P‖_∞ > C. This is weaker because it asks for existence of P (the ∃P direction), not the choice of y_i.
mathContext: Erdős's result: $\forall C > 0,\; \exists \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N,\; \forall n \geq N,\; \forall \mathbf{x} \in [-1,1]^m:\; \exists P,\; \deg P \leq n \wedge |P(x_i)| \leq 1\; \forall i \wedge \|P\|_{\infty} > C$. The key difference from the conjecture: here $P$ is existentially quantified (we find one bad polynomial), while the conjecture universally quantifies over $P$ (ALL polynomials matching $y$ are bad). The gap is the difference between $\exists P$ (constructive) and $\forall P$ (universal).

title: Lagrange Interpolation and Divergence
content: Two axioms: (1) Lagrange interpolation: given n distinct points, there is a unique polynomial of degree < n through all of them. (2) Lagrange divergence: there exist continuous functions for which interpolation on uniform nodes diverges — Runge's phenomenon.
mathContext:
**Lagrange**: $\forall$ distinct $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}$, $\forall y_1, \ldots, y_n$: $\exists! P \in \mathbb{R}[X],\; \deg P < n \wedge P(x_i) = y_i$. The formula is $P(x) = \sum_{i} y_i \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j}$.

**Divergence**: Faber (1914) showed for ANY node sequence, $\exists f \in C[-1,1]$ with $\|L_n f\|_{\infty} \to \infty$. For uniform nodes, Runge's example $f(x) = 1/(1+25x^2)$ gives wild oscillations near $\pm 1$. The Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_n = \|L_n\|$ grows as $\Omega(\log n)$ for any nodes.

title: Chebyshev Nodes and Optimality
content: Chebyshev nodes x_k = cos(π(2k+1)/(2n)) minimize the Lebesgue constant and give optimal polynomial interpolation behavior. The chebyshev_optimal axiom states: if |P(x_k)| ≤ 1 at all n+1 Chebyshev nodes and deg(P) = n, then ‖P‖_∞ ≤ 1.
mathContext: The Chebyshev nodes $x_k = \cos\frac{\pi(2k+1)}{2n}$ are roots of the Chebyshev polynomial $T_n(x) = \cos(n \arccos x)$. Their Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_n^{\text{Cheb}} = \frac{2}{\pi} \log n + O(1)$ is the smallest possible up to $O(1)$. The optimality axiom encodes: if $P$ is bounded at Chebyshev nodes, it's bounded everywhere. However, this does NOT resolve the conjecture because Chebyshev nodes are fixed — the adversary chooses arbitrary nodes.

title: exact_interpolation_case (Fully Proved)
content: For ε = 0 (exact interpolation): given n distinct points and arbitrary target values, Lagrange interpolation provides the unique polynomial of degree < n through all points. Proved by applying lagrange_interpolation axiom via Classical.choose_spec.
mathContext: This is the $\varepsilon = 0$ reduction: when ALL $n$ points must be matched and $\deg P < n$, the Lagrange polynomial is the unique solution. The conjecture for $\varepsilon = 0$ asks: can we choose $y_i$ so the Lagrange polynomial has $\|L_n\|_{\infty} > C$? Since $L_n(x) = \sum y_i \ell_i(x)$ where $\ell_i$ are the Lagrange basis polynomials, this asks: does $\max_i |\ell_i(x^*)| > C/n$ for some $x^*$? This is related to the Lebesgue constant.
